summary: Year 3 pupils mentally add or subtract ones to a three-digit number. The core insight: only the ones digit changes UNLESS the calculation bridges a ten, in which case the tens digit (and possibly the hundreds) also changes. Children anchor the hundreds and tens as a stable 'larger part' and operate only on the ones, reusing secure within-20 make-ten bonds for the bridging cases. Contrasting a non-bridging case directly with a bridging case is what refines the rough rule 'only the ones change' into the accurate 'only the ones change unless we cross a ten'.
misconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (adding the ones to the tens or hundreds digit)
Failing to bridge: 345+7 given as 342 or 3412 (keeps 2, drops the extra ten) instead of 352
Smaller-from-larger on the ones when subtracting bridges down (462−5 given as 463: does 5−2)
Believing 'only the ones digit ever changes', so bridging cases are mishandled

activities.title: Anchor the larger part, spin only the ones
steps: Show 345 on a place-value chart (e.g. a Gattegno chart) with the hundreds, tens and ones rows visible.
Work 345 + 3: change only the ones from 5 to 8, keeping '34_' fixed, and say aloud which digits stayed the same and which changed.
Name the value of each digit before adding (the 3 you add is three ones, so it joins the ones), to guard against adding to the wrong column.
Predict, before calculating, which digits will change.
activities.insight: A change to the ones stays local: the hundreds and tens act as an untouched anchor, so for a non-bridging case only the ones digit moves.

activities.title: Bridge a ten with make-ten bonds
steps: Work 345 + 7 on a marked number line (or a hundred-square segment near the decade): jump +5 to land on 350, then +2 more to reach 352.
Connect this to the within-20 bond already known: split 7 into 5 + 2, so 345 + 7 = 345 + 5 + 2.
Notice the moment the tens digit changes (4 becomes 5 as you cross 350) — this is the exception to 'only the ones change'.
Optionally watch a place-value chart where the ones roll past 9 and cascade a carry of +1 into the tens, with a number-line toggle showing the same jump onto 350 then stepping to 352.
activities.insight: When a calculation crosses a ten, the ones 'fill up' to the next decade and the tens digit also changes; make-ten bonds the child already knows handle the split.

activities.title: Contrast non-bridging and bridging side by side
steps: Place 345 + 3 and 345 + 7 next to each other and predict, for each, which digits will change before calculating.
Calculate both, then state which digits actually changed and why they differed.
Articulate the refined rule: 'only the ones change, unless we cross a ten'.
Try a mixed set of items sorted by whether they bridge, predicting each time.
activities.insight: Directly comparing a case where only the ones change with one that bridges turns the rough rule into the accurate rule and exposes the 'only the ones ever change' overgeneralisation.

activities.title: Bridge downwards when subtracting
steps: Work 462 − 5 on a number line (or hundred-square segment near the decade), moving DOWN: take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more to land on 457.
Check direction first: subtracting should make the answer smaller than 462, so an answer above 462 is wrong.
State which digits changed (the tens digit drops from 6 to 5) and why.
Thinking aloud, do 345 + 3, 345 + 7 and 462 − 5 in turn, saying which digits change after each.
activities.insight: Subtracting across a decade moves the number down past the ten, so the tens digit drops. A direction check catches the smaller-from-larger error when it gives an answer above the start (462 − 5 → 463), but it cannot catch every case. Checking that the tens digit dropped, because the answer passed below 460, makes the check complete.

checkQuestion: Ask the child to do these mentally, thinking aloud: 345 + 3, then 345 + 7, then 462 − 5. After each, ask which digits changed. Watch the two that bridge a ten.
checkAnswer: 348, 352, 457. 345+3 changes only the ones (348). 345+7 bridges: ones fill to 350 then +2 = 352 (tens digit also changes). 462−5 bridges down: 462−52 wait — take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more = 457 (tens digit changes).
